claims.text: The proposed lightweight high-entropy alloy can retain low density while providing the targeted properties.
An ultrafine, chemically homogeneous grain structure will give higher tensile strength than a coarse-grained baseline.
An ultrafine, chemically homogeneous grain structure will lower corrosion rates relative to a coarse-grained baseline.
An ultrafine, chemically homogeneous grain structure will reduce high-temperature oxidation weight gain relative to a coarse-grained baseline.
Chemical homogeneity suppresses deleterious precipitate formation.
The proposed benefits persist only while processing and service temperatures remain below the alloy's order-disorder transition.
The initial lightweight high-entropy alloy has a relatively coarse grain structure.
The initial alloy may exhibit elemental segregation.
Rapid solidification can refine the alloy's grains to the nanoscale.
Controlled dual-beam irradiation can refine grains to the nanoscale.
A high density of grain boundaries enhances vacancy-interstitial recombination.
The proposed defect-sink mechanism reduces the accumulation of dislocations.
The proposed defect-sink mechanism reduces precipitate accumulation.
Ballistic mixing maintains near-zero chemical short-range order and thereby preserves chemical homogeneity.
Traditional processing produces a coarser microstructure in the comparison alloy.
Traditional processing produces a more chemically heterogeneous microstructure in the comparison alloy.
Exposure above the order-disorder transition causes significant grain growth.
Exposure above the order-disorder transition causes elemental segregation.
Dominance of an alternative mechanism such as interstitial solid-solution strengthening diminishes the benefits attributable to grain refinement.
Crossing the order-disorder transition will cause performance to revert toward that of the baseline alloy.
